rungs.name: Occasional
rungs.label: Occasional
rungs.description: Done now and then, often only when prompted.

rungs.name: Developing

dimensions.name: Judgment
dimensions.subtitle: Critical Thinking
dimensions.description: Judgment is the ability to make sound decisions when the right answer is not obvious. These questions ask how you test your preferred options, check for bias, and learn from how your decisions turn out.
dimensions.pressing_question: What is the strongest argument against the option I prefer?
dimensions.summary_line: Making sound decisions when the right answer is not obvious.
dimensions.failure_line: Decisions follow the first preference and are neither tested nor reviewed.

guide.what: Judgment is the ability to make sound decisions when the right answer is not obvious. It shows in how a decision is made, not only in how it turns out, because a well-made decision can still end badly and a careless one can end well by luck. People with good judgment check whether common biases are shaping their views and set their preferred options into dialogue with the strongest possible counterarguments. After the decision has played out, they compare the results with what they expected and note what they would do differently next time.
guide.why: AI can produce a confident, well-written answer to almost any question within seconds. That makes it tempting to accept an answer without doing the work of deciding. As AI takes over more of the routine analytical work executives have been responsible for in the past, the contribution made by human leaders lies increasingly in choosing what should be done. Leaders who judge decisions only by their outcomes can learn the wrong lessons, because they cannot tell a sound decision that was unlucky from a careless one that happened to work.
guide.how: Judgment improves through practice on real decisions. Before a decision that matters, test your preferred option against the strongest counterarguments you can find, and check whether a bias is pulling you toward it. When the decision has played out, review how you made it as well as how it turned out, and record what you would change. Over time, those records show where your reasoning tends to go wrong.

items.label: Arguing against your preferred option
items.question: Before you make an important decision, how thoroughly do you work out the strongest argument against the option you currently prefer?
items.anchor_low_text: You usually go with the option you prefer without looking for the strongest case against it.
items.anchor_high_text: Before every important decision, you build the strongest case against your preferred option and weigh it seriously.
items.next_step: Before your next important decision, write down the strongest argument against the option you prefer. Hold your decision until you have thought deeply about whether the argument demands you change course.

items.label: Checking for bias
items.question: Before you commit to an important decision, how often do you check whether a cognitive bias is shaping your view, such as a reluctance to write off what you have already invested?
items.anchor_low_text: You rarely stop to ask whether a bias is shaping how you see a decision.
items.anchor_high_text: Before every important decision, you check for the biases most likely to affect it, such as a reluctance to write off past investment.
items.next_step: Think of a project or course of action you are deciding whether to continue. Ask yourself whether you would start it today if you had not already spent time and money on it. If the answer is no, consider whether that past investment is the main reason you are continuing.

items.label: Reviewing the outcome
items.question: Once an important decision has played out, how often do you compare the result with what you expected and note what you would do differently next time?
items.anchor_low_text: Once a decision is made, you rarely return to compare what happened with what you expected.
items.anchor_high_text: You review every important decision once it has played out and record what you would do differently.
items.next_step: Choose an important decision you made in the last six months. Write down what you expected to happen when you made it, what actually happened, and one thing you would do differently next time.

dimensions.name: Adaptability
dimensions.subtitle: Strategic Curiosity
dimensions.description: Adaptability means continuing to learn about your work by testing what you believe against what actually happens. These questions ask how you handle conflicting information, test new approaches, and keep your skills in use.
dimensions.pressing_question: What would I expect to see if my view were wrong?
dimensions.summary_line: Testing what you believe against what actually happens.
dimensions.failure_line: Views go untested, and demanding work is handed to AI by default.

guide.what: Adaptability means continuing to learn about your work by testing what you believe against what actually happens. Adaptable people treat their current views as the best explanation they have so far, not as settled facts. When new information conflicts with those views, they take the time to work out how seriously to take it. They try new approaches on a small scale before committing to them. They also keep doing the demanding parts of their work themselves in order to maintain the ability to judge the work done by others and by AI.
guide.why: Markets, technologies, and the organizations people work in change quickly, so views that were accurate a few years ago may no longer be true. People who stop testing what they believe end up acting on an out-of-date picture of their work. AI adds a second risk. When you hand a task to AI, you also hand over the thinking it required, and the skills behind it can weaken without your noticing. Someone who no longer does the work can lose the ability to tell whether AI has done it well.
guide.how: Adaptability is built through small, deliberate tests. Take one view you hold about your work, such as what a client values or why a process keeps failing. Decide what you would expect to see if you were wrong, then find a quick, low-cost way to check. Look honestly at the result, especially anything that does not fit, and adjust your view if the evidence calls for it.

items.label: Weighing new information
items.question: When a new data point conflicts with what you currently believe, how much effort do you spend working out how seriously you need to take it?
items.anchor_low_text: When new information conflicts with what you believe, you usually dismiss it or act on it without examining it.
items.anchor_high_text: When new information conflicts with what you believe, you examine it carefully before deciding whether to change your view.
items.next_step: The next time you come across information that conflicts with a view you hold about your work, check where it came from and whether other evidence supports it before you decide how much weight to give it.

items.label: Testing before committing
items.question: Before you commit to a new approach, how often do you test it first in a small, low-cost way?
items.anchor_low_text: You usually commit to a new approach in full without testing it first.
items.anchor_high_text: You test new approaches on a small scale, at low cost, before you commit to them.
items.next_step: Choose a change you are planning to make. Before you commit to it in full, try it on a small scale, such as with one team, one client, or one process, and review the results.

items.label: Keeping your skills in use
items.question: How often do you deliberately do the demanding part of a task yourself, to keep the skill, when AI could do it faster?
items.anchor_low_text: You hand demanding tasks to AI whenever it can do them faster.
items.anchor_high_text: You regularly do the demanding parts of your work yourself so that you keep the skills involved.
items.next_step: Choose a task you used to do yourself but now hand to AI, such as writing a first draft or analyzing a set of figures. Once a week, do that task yourself, then compare your result with what the AI produces.

dimensions.name: Empathy
dimensions.subtitle: Emotional Intelligence
dimensions.description: Empathy here means understanding the people you work with well enough to act on what you notice. These questions ask how you handle difficult conversations, from noticing that you are avoiding one to following up afterward.
dimensions.pressing_question: Which conversation am I putting off, and why?
dimensions.summary_line: Acting on what you notice about the people you work with.
dimensions.failure_line: Difficult conversations are avoided or handled only in writing.

guide.what: Empathy here means understanding the people you work with well enough to act on what you notice, including when acting is uncomfortable. It starts with recognizing when you are putting off a difficult conversation. It continues with having that conversation in person, where the other person can see that you mean what you say and you can see how it lands. It also includes checking back afterward to see how the other person is.
guide.why: AI tools make it easy to draft, soften, and send messages, and many exchanges no longer need a direct conversation at all. That convenience also makes it easier to avoid the conversations that are hardest to have, such as delivering criticism or admitting a mistake. AI can imitate a sympathetic tone, but it cannot take responsibility for what is said or notice how a colleague is really doing. When difficult conversations are put off, or held only in writing, problems between people tend to grow.
guide.how: Empathy develops through acting on real situations, one at a time. Name a conversation you have been putting off and be honest about what has stopped you. Decide what you want the conversation to achieve, set a date, and hold it in person or by phone. Afterward, check back with the other person to see how they are and what has changed.

items.label: Noticing avoidance
items.question: How quickly do you notice when you are putting off a difficult conversation at work?
items.anchor_low_text: You often realize late, or not at all, that you have been avoiding a difficult conversation.
items.anchor_high_text: You notice quickly when you are putting off a difficult conversation, and you can say why.
items.next_step: Make a list of the conversations at work that you have been putting off. Next to each one, note what has stopped you from having it.

items.label: Speaking directly
items.question: When something difficult needs to be said, how often do you say it in person rather than in writing?
items.anchor_low_text: You usually handle difficult messages in writing.
items.anchor_high_text: You say difficult things in person or by phone and keep writing for follow-up.
items.next_step: The next time you have something difficult to say that you would normally put in an email or chat message, say it in person or by phone instead.

items.label: Following up
items.question: After a difficult conversation, how often do you check back with the other person to see how they are?
items.anchor_low_text: Once a difficult conversation is over, you rarely return to it.
items.anchor_high_text: After every difficult conversation, you check back with the other person to see how they are.
items.next_step: Within a week of your next difficult conversation, check back with the other person. Ask how they are and whether there is anything about the conversation they want to discuss further.

dimensions.name: Conscience
dimensions.subtitle: Ethical Reasoning
dimensions.description: Conscience is the habit of examining what you are inclined to do before you act on it, when the question is one of right and wrong. These questions ask about self-interest, the balance between principles and people, and raising ethical concerns.
dimensions.pressing_question: What do I stand to gain, and who could be harmed?
dimensions.summary_line: Examining your inclinations when the question is one of right and wrong.
dimensions.failure_line: Ethical questions go unexamined or unraised.

guide.what: Conscience is the habit of examining what you are inclined to do before you act on it, when the question is one of right and wrong. It starts with asking whether your own interests are shaping what you think is right. It includes weighing the value of a principle against the harm that following it could cause to particular people. It also means speaking up when you believe something is ethically wrong, even when raising the concern will bring you into conflict with others.
guide.why: Decisions about AI often raise ethical questions that technical analysis cannot settle. AI systems pursue the goals they are given, and they cannot judge whether those goals, or the means used to reach them, are right. That judgment has to come from people. These questions rarely arrive labeled as ethical decisions. They come attached to deadlines, targets, and default settings, and there is usually pressure to go along. Someone who has not practiced examining their own motives, and speaking up, may not notice the question at all.
guide.how: Ethical reasoning becomes dependable through practice on real situations. Choose a situation in which you already know what you want to do. Ask what you stand to gain, consider who would be affected and how, and weigh the principle involved against any harm it could cause. Make the strongest case against your inclination before you decide. If you conclude that something is wrong, decide how and to whom you will say so, then review the outcome later.

items.label: Recognizing self-interest
items.question: When you face an ethical decision at work, how often do you ask whether your own interests are shaping what you think is right to do?
items.anchor_low_text: You rarely ask whether what you stand to gain is affecting your view of what is right.
items.anchor_high_text: In every ethical decision, you ask what you stand to gain and whether it is shaping your view.
items.next_step: The next time you face an ethical decision at work, write down what you personally stand to gain or lose from each option before you decide which to take.

items.label: Principles and People
items.question: When following a principle has the potential to cause harm to people, how carefully do you weigh the value of the principle against the harm to individuals before you decide what to do?
items.anchor_low_text: You decide without weighing the principle against the harm it could cause.
items.anchor_high_text: You weigh the value of the principle against the harm to the people affected before you decide.
items.next_step: Think of a rule or principle you follow at work that sometimes causes harm to particular people. Write down who is harmed and how, and what the rule or principle is meant to achieve. Then decide whether its value justifies that harm in the cases you have seen.

items.label: Raising ethical concerns
items.question: When you believe something at work is ethically wrong, how often do you say so, even if raising the concern would bring you into conflict with others?
items.anchor_low_text: You usually keep ethical concerns to yourself when raising them would cause conflict.
items.anchor_high_text: You raise ethical concerns whenever you have them, even when doing so causes conflict.
items.next_step: If you have an ethical concern at work that you have not raised, decide who needs to hear it and what you will say. Then set a date by which you will raise it.

dimensions.name: Imagination
dimensions.subtitle: Creative Thinking
dimensions.description: Imagination is the ability to bring something to a task that would not be there without you. These questions ask how you work with AI and where you look for ideas.
dimensions.pressing_question: What does my version add that the model's does not?
dimensions.summary_line: Bringing something to your work that would not be there without you.
dimensions.failure_line: The central idea of important work comes from AI.

guide.what: Imagination is the ability to bring something to a task that would not be there without you. When you use AI, this means forming the central concept yourself before you consult a model, and then adding your own thinking rather than settling for what the tool produces. It also means drawing on knowledge from outside your own field, since many breakthroughs come from connecting insights that specialists in a single discipline have not thought to combine.
guide.why: AI can produce a competent first draft of almost any document, plan, or analysis in seconds. Because it works by recombining patterns that already exist in its training data, it tends to produce relatively predictable outputs. As a result, when many people use the same tools to develop their thinking, their ideas start to look alike. The value a leader adds increasingly lies in the contributions they can make that a model would not have been able to generate.
guide.how: Start important work by setting down your own view of the main idea before you open an AI tool. Then use AI to test that view, find its weak points, or fill in detail, rather than to replace it. Compare your version with the one a model produces and identify what yours adds. Look regularly beyond your own field, at how people in other disciplines approach similar problems.

items.label: Thinking first
items.question: How often do you work out the main idea of important work yourself before you use AI?
items.anchor_low_text: You usually start important work by asking AI for the main idea.
items.anchor_high_text: You work out the main idea of important work yourself before you use AI.
items.next_step: For your next important piece of work, write down your main idea in a few sentences before you open an AI tool. Then use AI to test or develop that idea, not to replace it.

items.label: Adding your own ideas
items.question: When working with AI, how often do you add an idea of your own to important work rather than relying on the version the model produces?
items.anchor_low_text: You usually accept the version AI produces with only light editing.
items.anchor_high_text: You consistently add ideas of your own to what AI produces before the work goes out.
items.next_step: Before you share the next piece of work that AI helped you produce, identify at least one idea in it that came from you rather than the model. If you cannot find one, add one before you share the work.

items.label: Drawing on other fields
items.question: When you work on a problem, how often do you draw on ideas from outside your own field?
items.anchor_low_text: You usually draw only on ideas from your own field.
items.anchor_high_text: You regularly look to other fields for ideas when you work on a problem.
items.next_step: Choose a problem you are working on and find out how people in a different field handle similar problems, by reading an article or book or by talking to someone in that field.

dimensions.name: Authenticity
dimensions.subtitle: Personal Sovereignty
dimensions.description: Authenticity involves acting on your own judgment, and it is tested most when your situation is uncertain. These questions ask how you handle worry, prepare for the worst outcome, and decide what to do next.
dimensions.pressing_question: What would I do if I were not worried?
dimensions.summary_line: Acting on your own judgment when the outcome is uncertain.
dimensions.failure_line: Worry, events, or other people decide what happens next.

guide.what: Authenticity involves acting on your own judgment, and it is tested most when your situation is uncertain. Uncertainty can push people to act based on their worries or to wait until events or others decide for them. Maintaining personal sovereignty means being prepared to respond to the worst outcomes, but not allowing your worries to limit your scope of action.
guide.why: In uncertain situations, it is tempting to hand a decision to someone or something else. AI tools offer confident recommendations, colleagues offer a consensus view, and worry points toward whatever seems safest. Each can be a useful input. But a leader who lets any of them make the decision is no longer acting on their own judgment, and the people they lead lose the benefit of that judgment when they need it most.
guide.how: Take an uncertain situation you face now and write down what you think you should do, and why, before you ask AI or anyone else for a view. Then note what concerns you about the situation and how those concerns are influencing you. Work out in concrete terms how you would respond if the worst outcome happened, so that fear of it no longer limits the options you are willing to consider. Treat advice from colleagues and analysis from AI as inputs, and then make the decision yourself.

items.label: Keeping worry in its place
items.question: When you are worried about how a situation at work will turn out, how well do you keep that worry from deciding what you do?
items.anchor_low_text: Worry about how things will turn out often decides what you do.
items.anchor_high_text: You notice your worries and keep them from deciding what you do.
items.next_step: Choose a situation at work that worries you. Write down what you are worried about and one thing you are doing, or avoiding, because of that worry. Then ask whether you would act the same way if you were not worried.

items.label: Planning for the worst case
items.question: When you are worried that something at work will go badly, how often do you plan out how you would respond if the worst outcome happened?
items.anchor_low_text: You rarely work out how you would respond if the worst outcome happened.
items.anchor_high_text: When something worries you, you work out in concrete terms how you would respond to the worst outcome.
items.next_step: Think of a situation at work you are worried about and identify the worst realistic outcome. Write down, step by step, how you would respond if it happened.

items.label: Deciding for yourself
items.question: When you cannot know how things will turn out, how often do you decide your next step yourself, rather than waiting for events or other people to decide it?
items.anchor_low_text: When the outcome is uncertain, you usually wait for events or other people to decide.
items.anchor_high_text: When the outcome is uncertain, you decide your next step yourself and act on it.
items.next_step: Think of a situation at work in which you have been waiting for events or other people to decide what happens next. Write down what you think you should do and why, then take the first step yourself.

correlation_metrics.label: Hours a week using AI tools

habitual.note: Most practices are habitual across all six skills.

developing.note: Practices are developing, with some inconsistency.

occasional.note: Practices appear now and then but are not yet habits.

analytical.note: Strong on judgment and testing ideas, weaker on difficult conversations.

peopleLed.note: Strong on people and ethics, weaker on testing ideas and independent thinking.

starting.note: Most practices are not yet part of how they work.
